questions.q: What are two examples of observations you should record in your weather diary?
questions.a: Temperature and wind direction (or rainfall/cloud cover). A wrong answer suggests the student confuses weather with general climate or forgets the specific measurable elements mentioned in the definition.

questions.q: Why is it important to record weather at the same time every day?
questions.a: It ensures the data is consistent and comparable, allowing you to see true changes rather than differences caused by the time of day. If a student thinks it doesn't matter, they fail to understand the concept of "fair comparison" in data collection.

questions.q: If you notice that the temperature drops every time the wind starts blowing from the north, what have you successfully created?
questions.a: You have identified a weather pattern. A wrong answer shows the student views the diary as a list of random events rather than a tool for logical connection.

questions.q: How does keeping a diary over three months change your understanding compared to just looking at the sky for one day?
questions.a: A single day shows current conditions, while three months reveal trends and patterns that repeat. A wrong answer suggests the student struggles to distinguish between a snapshot of weather and a series of observations.

questions.q: If your diary shows it rained every day for a week, is it accurate to say the "climate" of your city is rainy? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, because climate represents long-term averages (years), whereas a week is just a temporary weather event. A wrong answer indicates confusion between weather (short-term) and climate (long-term).

questions.q: Imagine you want to know if mornings are usually windier than afternoons; how would you design your diary entry to test this?
questions.a: The student should propose recording wind observations at two specific times (morning and afternoon) consistently for several days. A poor answer fails to incorporate the "consistency" or "time-variable" needed for a fair comparison.
